Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The search will continue until at least Friday night for 16 people missing since Thursday morning when a helicopter carrying them to an offshore oil platform ditched in the Atlantic Ocean off Newfoundland, Canadian officials said. A helicopter made an emergency crash landing off Newfoundland en route to Hibernia oil field on Thursday. One survivor, identified as Robert Decker, was found and taken to a hospital, but efforts to find more survivors had proven fruitless, said Maj. Denis McGuire of the Rescue Coordination Center in Halifax, Nova Scotia. The body of one person, who has not been identified publicly, also was pulled from the water. There were 18 people aboard the helicopter when it went down, about 30 nautical miles from St. John's. "All we've got is the debris field," McGuire said. "There are no indications of any [more] survivors, but the search will continue." The water is 400 feet deep at the site where the helicopter hit the water, he said. Helicopters and ships were scouring the debris field Thursday evening, and search-and-rescue technicians were planning to use night-vision goggles and flares overnight. The debris filled a six-mile area, said Jeri Grychowski of the Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax. Officials became aware that the helicopter was having problems shortly after 9:10 a.m., when the pilot declared a mayday, McGuire said. "They declared their mayday and then they hit the water or landed in the water approximately eight minutes later," he said. About 25 minutes later, a helicopter arrived and discovered the survivor, the body, the overturned helicopter and two empty life rafts, he said. Those aboard should have have been wearing survival suits that would have kept them dry and were equipped with lights and personal locator beacons, but the suits have not helped searchers. "We have not received any signals whatsoever," McGuire said. The suits theoretically would allow wearers to survive 24 hours in the freezing waters -- or until about 9 a.m. Friday -- but the search effort was to continue well beyond that. "We will continue to search until there's absolutely no chance that any survivors will be located," he said. "Until last light [Friday]." At that time, based on water temperature and the size of the search area, officials will decide whether to continue the effort, he said. Early in the day, high winds and seas hampered the search, but by late afternoon, the weather had improved, though seas were still about 13 to 16 feet (4 to 5 meters) and winds were at about 40 knots (46 mph). The survivor was taken to the Health Sciences Center in St. John's, Newfoundland. The helicopter had been heading to the Hibernia offshore oil platform when it went down in what Grychowski called a controlled emergency crash landing. The pilot reported some technical malfunctions before the crash and radioed that he was turning the chopper around, said Rick Burt of Cougar Helicopters -- the operator of the S-92 Sikorsky copter.

(CNN) -- Canadian authorities announced that search operations would persist through Friday evening for 16 individuals still unaccounted for after their helicopter went down in Atlantic waters near Newfoundland on Thursday morning while transporting them to an offshore drilling platform.

The aircraft crash-landed during an emergency situation while flying toward the Hibernia oil field. Rescue teams located a single survivor—Robert Decker—who was transported to a medical facility, though subsequent attempts to locate additional survivors yielded nothing, according to Major Denis McGuire from the Halifax-based Rescue Coordination Center in Nova Scotia. Searchers also recovered one deceased individual from the water, though this person's identity has not been released to the public.

The helicopter had carried 18 passengers and crew members when it plunged into the sea roughly 30 nautical miles from St. John's. "What we're left with is essentially a debris field," McGuire explained. "Nothing suggests there are additional survivors, yet we're continuing our search efforts."

At the crash site, ocean depths reach approximately 400 feet, according to McGuire. Throughout Thursday evening, aircraft and vessels combed through the scattered wreckage, with rescue specialists preparing to employ night-vision equipment and flares once darkness fell. Jeri Grychowski, also with the Halifax Rescue Coordination Centre, indicated that debris was scattered across a six-mile stretch.

Trouble first became apparent around 9:10 a.m. when the pilot issued a mayday call, McGuire reported. "Roughly eight minutes following that mayday call, they either crashed into or made a landing on the water," he stated. A rescue helicopter arrived on scene approximately 25 minutes afterward, discovering the sole survivor, the deceased passenger, the capsized aircraft, and a pair of unoccupied life rafts.

Passengers and crew were supposed to be outfitted in survival suits designed to keep wearers dry and equipped with illumination devices and personal locator beacons—equipment that has thus far provided no assistance to search crews. "There's been absolutely no signal detected," McGuire noted.

These suits are theoretically capable of sustaining someone in frigid waters for a full day, meaning survival chances would extend to roughly 9 a.m. Friday—though rescue efforts were slated to continue past this window. "We won't stop searching until there's zero possibility of finding survivors," McGuire affirmed, adding operations would run "until the last light of day Friday." Officials will then evaluate whether to extend the search further, weighing factors like ocean temperature and the search zone's dimensions.

Morning conditions featured strong winds and rough seas that complicated rescue efforts, though conditions eased somewhat by late afternoon—waves remained substantial at 13 to 16 feet (4 to 5 meters), with winds still gusting around 40 knots (46 mph).

Doctors at St. John's Health Sciences Center in Newfoundland received the survivor for treatment. Grychowski characterized the incident as a controlled emergency landing that occurred as the helicopter made its way to the Hibernia platform. Rick Burt, representing Cougar Helicopters (the company operating the S-92 Sikorsky aircraft), noted that the pilot had reported experiencing technical difficulties prior to the crash and had radioed intentions to turn the aircraft around.

A helicopter transporting 18 people to the Hibernia offshore oil platform went down in the Atlantic Ocean off the coast of Newfoundland on Thursday morning, triggering an extensive search and rescue operation that authorities indicated would likely continue into Friday night and possibly beyond.

The aircraft, en route to the massive oil production facility located in the frigid waters off Canada's eastern coast, experienced a catastrophic failure that forced it to ditch into the ocean. The incident immediately mobilized search and rescue teams, who worked against difficult conditions and the constant threat posed by the cold North Atlantic waters to those who may have survived the initial impact.

## One Survivor Found, One Body Recovered

Amid the search efforts, rescuers located one survivor, identified as Robert Decker, who was pulled from the water and transported to a hospital for treatment. In addition to the survivor, searchers recovered the body of one unidentified individual from the ocean, confirming the worst fears about the severity of the crash.

## Debris Field Discovered, Hopes for Additional Survivors Dim

Despite mounting a comprehensive search operation involving multiple vessels and aircraft, officials were only able to locate a debris field stretching across six miles of ocean. Among the wreckage, search teams found the helicopter itself, overturned in the water, along with two life rafts that had deployed but were found empty. The absence of any other survivors within this debris field raised serious concerns among officials about the fate of the remaining passengers and crew, though the search continued in hopes of finding more survivors.

## Timeline of the Emergency

Investigators pieced together a timeline of the disaster based on communications from the aircraft. The helicopter's pilot issued a mayday call at approximately 9:10 a.m., signaling that the aircraft was in distress. Just eight minutes later, the helicopter struck the water's surface. Rescue crews managed to arrive at the crash site roughly 25 minutes after the impact, a response time that, while relatively swift, still left a critical window during which those aboard would have been exposed to the Atlantic's dangerous conditions.

## Survival Equipment Raises Questions

All passengers aboard the flight had been equipped with specialized survival suits designed specifically for scenarios like this one. These suits are engineered to keep wearers dry and to sustain life for up to 24 hours even in freezing ocean waters, addressing the extreme hypothermia risk posed by the North Atlantic. The suits also come equipped with safety lights and personal locator beacons intended to help rescuers pinpoint the location of anyone who ended up in the water.

However, in a troubling development for search and rescue coordinators, officials reported that no signals from these personal locator beacons had been detected by search teams. This absence of beacon signals added another layer of uncertainty to the operation, as searchers were left without a key tool that could have helped guide them to survivors who may have been drifting in the vast expanse of ocean.

As the search entered its second day, officials continued to grapple with the difficult reality of the situation—balancing the slim hope of finding additional survivors against the harsh conditions and the troubling lack of signals from safety equipment specifically designed to prevent such tragedies.

# Helicopter Carrying Oil Platform Crew Crashes Off Newfoundland Coast; Search and Rescue Underway

**ST. JOHN'S, Newfoundland and Labrador** — A helicopter transporting workers to an offshore oil platform crashed into the frigid waters of the North Atlantic on Thursday morning, prompting a massive search and rescue operation involving the Canadian Coast Guard, military aircraft, and nearby commercial vessels.

The Sikorsky S-92 helicopter, operated by a charter company under contract with an offshore energy consortium, was en route to a production platform roughly 170 nautical miles southeast of St. John's when it lost contact with air traffic controllers shortly before 9:30 a.m. local time. The aircraft was carrying 18 people, including a two-person flight crew and 16 oil workers, according to officials from the company operating the platform.

"We received a distress signal indicating a mechanical issue shortly before radar contact was lost," said a spokesperson for the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre in Halifax. "Search assets were mobilized immediately."

## Rescue Efforts

Two Cormorant search-and-rescue helicopters were dispatched from Canadian Forces Base Gander, alongside a fixed-wing Hercules aircraft to assist in locating survivors amid choppy seas and temperatures hovering just above freezing. The Canadian Coast Guard vessel *Ann Harvey*, which had been operating in the vicinity, reached the crash site within the first hour and began pulling survivors from the water.

By early afternoon, officials confirmed that seven survivors had been recovered and transported to hospitals in St. John's, with several reported to be suffering from hypothermia and injuries consistent with impact trauma. Rescue crews continued searching for the remaining passengers as darkness approached, though hopes for additional survivors dimmed given the water temperature, which experts say can lead to severe hypothermia within minutes.

"Every moment counts in these conditions," said Coast Guard Commander Lisa Whalen. "Our crews are doing everything possible, but the North Atlantic this time of year is unforgiving."

## Survivor Accounts

One survivor, identified by family members as 34-year-old mechanical engineer Derek Coombs, was reported in stable condition at St. John's General Hospital. His sister, speaking briefly to reporters outside the hospital, said Coombs recalled the helicopter shuddering violently before losing power.

"He said everything happened so fast — an alarm, then the aircraft just dropped," she said. "He was lucky to get his suit sealed and get out before it went under."

Offshore workers in the region are required to wear specialized survival suits during helicopter transport, a safety measure credited with helping several passengers stay afloat long enough to be rescued.

## Industry and Government Response

The operator of the offshore platform issued a statement expressing condolences to families and pledging full cooperation with investigators. "Our thoughts are with all those affected by this tragedy," the statement read. "The safety of our workforce is our highest priority, and we are working closely with search and rescue teams and regulatory authorities."

Canada's Transportation Safety Board announced it would launch a full investigation into the cause of the crash, examining maintenance records, weather conditions, and communications data from the aircraft's final minutes.

Premier of Newfoundland and Labrador Andrew Furey addressed reporters Thursday evening, calling the crash "a devastating blow" to the province's close-knit offshore energy community. "Many of these workers are neighbors, friends, family members of people across this province," Furey said. "We are praying for the safe recovery of all those still missing."

This is not the first such incident in the region; a similar helicopter crash in 2009 killed 17 people, prompting sweeping safety reforms in offshore helicopter transport across Atlantic Canada.

Search efforts are expected to continue through the night, with additional vessels and aircraft joining the operation as weather conditions allow.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
